# Sources ledger: history-r2 (topic discovery)

Read sources first (S1-S5), then leads seen only in search summaries or through another source (S6-S13).
A search summary is recorded as a lead, never used as evidence.

### S1. Jukka Tuhkuri (Aalto University), "Why did Endurance sink?", Polar Record vol. 61, e23, Cambridge University Press, published online 6 October 2025
- Primary: the study itself (peer-reviewed research article, open access, CC BY 4.0). It compares Endurance's structure with that of the early Antarctic ships, using their drawings and dimensions and the expedition's letters and diaries as quoted. The author is an ice-mechanics engineer, not a historian. URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/polar-record/article/why-did-endurance-sink/6CC2C2D56087035A94DEB50930B81980
- Access: read (the full article body, abstract to conclusions, in the first 100,000 characters of the page; the reference list was not read)
- Supports: C26, C27, C28, C29, C30, C31. Counterevidence: the paper itself cites Bound (2022) as still giving the rudder as the sole cause (C29). It calls its own method a "simple structural analysis" from dimensional relations and assumes similar timber across the ships. It says side damage "may be buried in the mud" and "we may never know", and it calls why Shackleton chose the ship "not known". I read nothing that independently corroborates the structural finding.
- Status: primary record of one study. Its 1915 dates rest on the expedition records it cites, which I did not see.

### S2. Allison Marsh (historian, University of South Carolina), "The First Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Was a Bold, Beautiful Failure", IEEE Spectrum (Past Forward series), 31 October 2019, corrected 1 February 2021
- Secondary: a historian's account in an engineering society's magazine. It draws on the 1857-58 expedition logbooks and on Donard de Cogan's 1985 analysis of the cable (S7). URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/tech-history/heroic-failures/the-first-transatlantic-telegraph-cable-was-a-bold-beautiful-failure
- Access: read (the full article text; the reader comments under it were not used)
- Supports: C01, C02, C03, C04, C05, C07, C08, C12, C14, C17, C19, C20, C21, C22, C23, C24. Counterevidence: it reports de Cogan's view that the cable's manufacture and storage made failure likely whatever Whitehouse did (C19), against the commission's verdict (C08). As I read it, it words Thomson's law as "inversely proportional to the square of the cable's length". That is the reverse of S4 and of the physics, so I treat it as a slip for the signalling speed and use S4's wording.
- Status: credible secondary. It is the only read source for C04, C20, C23 and C24.

### S3. William B. Ashworth Jr. (consultant for the History of Science, Linda Hall Library; emeritus associate professor of history, University of Missouri-Kansas City), "Scientist of the Day: E.O. Wildman Whitehouse", Linda Hall Library, 1 October 2024
- Secondary: a short essay by a historian of science. URL: https://lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/e-o-wildman-whitehouse
- Access: read (the full post)
- Supports: C01, C03, C05, C06, C07, C08, C09, C10, C11, C17, C18, C19, C21. Counterevidence: it reports critics who say the cable "was doomed from the start, because it was shoddily made, improperly stored" and that Whitehouse was made "the scapegoat" (C19). The author answers "We don't know", and he doubts Whitehouse would have succeeded anyway. Its line "Both 1865 and 1866 cables succeeded" is compressed: what I read does not describe the 1865 attempt, so its fate is unverified. It recommends Bruce J. Hunt, Imperial Science (2021, S8) as the fairest treatment.
- Status: credible secondary, independent of S2 (different author and venue, and I saw no shared citation). It is the only read source for C06 (the 1858 half), C09, C11 and C18.

### S4. University of Glasgow Library, Special Collections, "Lord Kelvin: Atlantic Cable" (web exhibition; first exhibited 1977, adapted for the web 2008)
- Secondary: an institutional exhibition text built on the Kelvin Papers. The papers themselves are primary, but I saw only the captions and short letter excerpts. URL: https://www.gla.ac.uk/myglasgow/library/files/special/exhibns/Kelvin/atlanticcable.html
- Access: read (the Atlantic Cable section, its captions and excerpts from six letters; the rest of the exhibition was not read)
- Supports: C01, C02, C03, C06, C07, C10, C12, C13, C14, C15, C16, C17, C21, C22, C25. Counterevidence: its cause of failure ("several thousand volts" that "burned the cable out") is the inquiry's view. The text dates from 1977, before de Cogan's reassessment (C19).
- Status: credible institutional secondary, on an older text. It is the only read source for C13, C15, C16 and C25.

### S5. J. Leslie Price (University of Hull), review of Anne Goldgar, "Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age" (University of Chicago Press, 2007), Reviews in History no. 666, Institute of Historical Research, April 2008
- Secondary: a scholarly review of an archival study. URL: https://reviews.history.ac.uk/review/666
- Access: read (the full review; a closing line says the author accepts the review)
- Supports: C32, C33, C34, C35. Counterevidence: the review names no archives, prices or court cases, and it calls the book's discussion of collecting "rather speculative". It names no economist or historian who disagrees. A disagreement is hinted at only in a search summary of S6, which I could not read.
- Status: credible secondary about a study I did not read. The book itself was not read.

### S6. Anne Goldgar, "Tulipmania: An Overblown Crisis?", History Today (date not seen)
- Secondary: the historian's own popular article on her archive work. URL: https://www.historytoday.com/node/54516
- Access: snippet (the page refused automated reading with HTTP 403, so I saw only a search summary)
- Supports: no claim. Counterevidence: the search summary says the article notes that other historians have long described the crash as a serious economic disaster. That is unread, so it is not used.
- Status: lead only.

### S7. Donard de Cogan, analysis of the 1858 cable and of Whitehouse's part in its failure (1985)
- Secondary: an analysis of how the cable was made and of the records. No URL seen.
- Access: indirect (known only through S2's account of it)
- Supports: C19 and C20, only through S2. Counterevidence: the 1861 inquiry (C08) and S4.
- Status: unread. Read it, or Hunt (S8), before the beat that reopens the verdict is recorded.

### S8. Bruce J. Hunt, "Imperial Science: Cable Telegraphy and Electrical Physics in the Victorian British Empire", Cambridge University Press, 2021
- Secondary: a scholarly monograph by a historian of physics. URL seen: https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108902700.002 (a chapter page)
- Access: snippet (a search summary quoted "There were many reasons why the first Atlantic cable failed and many reasons why blame for its failure came to be apportioned as it was."; S3 recommends the book)
- Supports: no claim yet.
- Status: lead. It is the best next read for C04, C11, C19, the inquiry's formal name, the 1866 cable's design and its signalling speed.

### S9. Royal Society archive, "Unpublished extract of a letter, 'On the theory of the electric telegraph', from William Thomson to Gabriel George Stokes" (AP/37/22)
- Primary: the archive record of Thomson's own derivation. An abstract of his paper is said to have been printed in Proceedings of the Royal Society vol. 7. URL: https://makingscience.royalsociety.org/items/ap_37_22/unpublished-extract-of-a-letter-on-the-theory-of-the-electric-telegraph-from-william-thomson-to-gabriel-george-stokes
- Access: snippet (search summary only; the summaries disagree on whether it dates from 1854 or 1855)
- Supports: no claim. C12 rests on S2 and S4.
- Status: lead to the primary record for C12.

### S10. Science Museum Group collection, "Whitehouse's induction coil, 1858" (object co32894)
- Primary: a museum's record of the surviving object. URL: https://collection.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects/co32894/whitehouses-induction-coil-1858-coil
- Access: snippet (seen only as a search result title)
- Supports: no claim.
- Status: lead. It is the picture reference for the coil's real shape, to check before that still is made.

### S11. CNN, "Historical mysteries solved by science in 2025" (syndicated, 23 December 2025)
- Popular: a news roundup. URL: https://abc17news.com/cnn-other/2025/12/23/historical-mysteries-solved-by-science-in-2025/

- Supports: no claim. It is where the Endurance lead (S1) and several dropped leads came from (notes.md).

### S12. NPR, report on Tuhkuri's Endurance study, 8 October 2025
- Popular: a news report. URL: https://www.npr.org/2025/10/08/nx-s1-5564788/antarctica-ernest-shackleton-ship-endurance-research-south-pole

- Supports: no claim.

### S13. Smithsonian Magazine, "There Never Was a Real Tulip Fever" (date not seen)
- Popular: a magazine article quoting Goldgar. URL: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/there-never-was-real-tulip-fever-180964915/
